description: Carbon fibre, Kevlar, GRP, geotextiles, micro-fibres and wearable textile electronics.
content_html:
What Are Composite Materials?

Composite materials are engineered by combining two or more different materials. One material acts as the reinforcement (providing strength or stiffness) and the other acts as the matrix (binding the reinforcement together and protecting it). Neither component alone has all the properties of the finished composite. This is why composites can outperform conventional metals or polymers for specific applications.

Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP)

Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) combines carbon fibre strands with a polymer matrix — typically epoxy resin. Carbon fibres are made by heating polyacrylonitrile (PAN) at high temperatures in a controlled atmosphere until most non-carbon atoms are driven off, leaving a fibre that is almost pure carbon. These fibres have very high tensile strength and stiffness but are brittle on their own. The epoxy resin matrix binds the fibres, distributes loads between them and protects them from impact and chemical attack.

CFRP is significantly lighter than steel for the same structural strength, making it essential in applications where weight saving is critical. Airbus uses CFRP extensively in modern commercial aircraft — the wings and fuselage sections of aircraft such as the A350 are predominantly CFRP, reducing aircraft weight and therefore fuel consumption per passenger. It is also used in Formula 1 monocoques, high-performance bicycle frames and sporting equipment.

Key Fact

CFRP has a very high strength-to-weight ratio — it is stiffer and stronger than steel by weight, while being significantly lighter. This property is why Airbus uses it in aircraft structures, reducing fuel consumption. Its disadvantages include high manufacturing cost and difficulty of repair after impact damage.

Kevlar (Para-Aramid Fibre)

Kevlar is a synthetic para-aramid fibre developed by DuPont. It has exceptionally high tensile strength — around five times stronger than steel by weight — and outstanding toughness (resistance to tearing and impact). Unlike CFRP, Kevlar is not brittle; it absorbs energy by deforming rather than shattering. This makes it the preferred material for personal protective equipment: body armour (bullet-resistant vests), cut-resistant gloves for food processing and industrial use, and motorcycle protective clothing.

Kevlar is also used as reinforcement in composite structures where impact resistance is important — for example, in the hulls of racing kayaks and in aerospace structures where bird-strike resistance is required. It can be combined with carbon fibre in a hybrid composite to balance stiffness (from CFRP) with toughness (from Kevlar).

Glass-Reinforced Plastic (GRP)

Glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) uses glass fibre as the reinforcement within a polyester or epoxy resin matrix. It is cheaper and easier to manufacture than CFRP. GRP is corrosion-resistant, mouldable into complex shapes and has a good strength-to-weight ratio (though lower than CFRP). It is used for boat hulls, surf and kayak shells, car body panels (notably on classic sports cars), storage tanks and low-cost architectural cladding panels.

The table below compares the three main composites:

Material Reinforcement Key property Typical use
CFRPCarbon fibreVery high stiffness and strength-to-weightAircraft structures, racing cars
Kevlar (KFRP)Para-aramid fibreVery high toughness and impact resistanceBody armour, cut-resistant gloves
GRPGlass fibreGood strength-to-weight, corrosion-resistant, lower costBoat hulls, car panels, tanks

Technical Textiles

Technical textiles are designed for performance rather than appearance. They are engineered to meet specific requirements in demanding applications: protection, filtration, moisture management or structural reinforcement.

Geotextiles

Geotextiles are permeable fabrics used in civil engineering. They are laid in the ground to separate, filter, reinforce or drain soil. A road built over soft ground may have a geotextile layer between the sub-soil and the gravel base to prevent mixing while still allowing water to drain through. Geotextiles are typically made from polypropylene or polyester and are produced in woven or non-woven forms depending on the required balance of strength and permeability.

Micro-Fibres

Micro-fibres are synthetic fibres with a diameter of less than one denier — finer than a strand of silk. The fine structure creates a very dense weave with billions of tiny air pockets, making micro-fibre fabrics soft, lightweight and highly effective at moisture management. They are used in sports clothing (wicking away sweat to keep athletes dry and comfortable), in microfibre cleaning cloths (the fine fibres mechanically trap dirt and bacteria without needing chemical cleaners), and in waterproof breathable membranes.

Interactive and Wearable Textile Electronics

Wearable electronics embed electronic functionality into textiles without making them rigid or unwearable. Methods include: weaving conductive metallic yarns into fabric to create circuits; attaching flexible printed circuit boards to the textile; and integrating sensors, LEDs or heating elements directly into clothing. Applications include: sports performance garments with heart rate and motion sensors; heated motorcycle and ski clothing; and electroluminescent safety vests for cyclists and construction workers.

The key challenge in wearable electronics is durability — the electronics must survive washing, stretching and the mechanical stresses of wear. Encapsulation (covering components in a flexible protective coating) and careful choice of washable conductive materials are the main technical solutions.

Key Fact

Technical textiles covered in this unit include geotextiles (civil engineering — road and drainage), micro-fibres (sports clothing and cleaning), breathable membranes (outdoor gear), and interactive textiles (wearable electronics in sports and safety garments).

Breathable membranes such as PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) expanded membranes work by having pores large enough to allow water vapour (sweat) to escape but small enough to block liquid water droplets. This one-way passage makes the fabric waterproof while remaining breathable. Moisture management fabrics use capillary action: a hydrophobic inner layer (repelling liquid water) sits against the skin and pushes moisture outward into a hydrophilic outer layer that spreads it over a wide surface area for rapid evaporation. Sun-protective clothing uses tightly woven or coated fabrics with a UV Protection Factor (UPF) rating, blocking UV radiation from reaching the skin.
exam_tip_html: For questions comparing composites, always name the reinforcement and matrix materials, not just the composite. ‘CFRP uses carbon fibre in an epoxy resin matrix’ is more creditworthy than ‘carbon fibre is strong and light.’ For technical textiles questions, link the fabric structure to the function it achieves — for example, ‘micro-fibre’s very fine diameter creates billions of tiny air pockets that trap dirt mechanically without chemicals.’ Always name at least one specific application when the question asks you to explain why a material is suitable.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Composites combine a reinforcement (e.g. carbon, glass or aramid fibre) with a matrix (e.g. epoxy resin) to achieve properties neither component has alone. CFRP is used in aircraft (Airbus) for its stiffness-to-weight ratio; Kevlar provides toughness for body armour; GRP is the lower-cost option for boat hulls and car panels.
  • Technical textiles are engineered for performance: geotextiles for civil engineering, micro-fibres for moisture management, breathable membranes for waterproof-breathable clothing, and interactive textiles for wearable electronics in sports and safety applications.
  • In exam answers, name the reinforcement and matrix for composites, and link the fabric structure to the specific function it achieves for technical textiles.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of the matrix in a composite material?
A) It provides high tensile strength and stiffness
B) It binds the reinforcement, distributes loads and protects it from damage
C) It adds UV resistance to the composite
D) It replaces the need for reinforcement fibres in load-bearing applications
practice_questions.marks: B) It binds the reinforcement, distributes loads and protects it from damage [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the reinforcement material and the matrix material used in GRP.
practice_questions.marks:
• Reinforcement: glass fibre [1 mark]
• Matrix: polyester resin OR epoxy resin [1 mark]
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two properties of Kevlar that make it suitable for use in body armour.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks (1 per property, plus 1 for development of one):
• Very high tensile strength — roughly five times stronger than steel by weight — meaning a bullet cannot easily pass through the fibres (1).
• High toughness / impact resistance — it absorbs energy by deforming rather than shattering, spreading the impact across a larger area of the vest (1).
• Lightweight — being lighter than equivalent steel protection, it allows the wearer to move freely (1).
[Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why CFRP is used by Airbus in aircraft structures rather than steel. Refer to specific material properties in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per developed point:
• CFRP has a much higher strength-to-weight ratio than steel (1), meaning structural components can be made lighter, reducing the overall aircraft weight and therefore fuel burn per passenger (1).
• CFRP is resistant to corrosion unlike steel (1), which reduces maintenance requirements and avoids the mass of protective coatings needed on steel structures (1).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the suitability of CFRP and GRP for the hull of a racing yacht. Consider cost, weight, strength and manufacturing in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for developed comparative points (not just listing one material's properties):
• CFRP is significantly lighter than GRP for the same structural strength (1), which is critical for a racing yacht where speed depends on minimising displacement (1).
• GRP is considerably cheaper to produce than CFRP because glass fibre costs less than carbon fibre and the resin can be applied by hand lay-up without autoclave curing (1).
• CFRP is more difficult to repair after impact damage (it shatters rather than deforming); GRP can be patched more easily with additional resin and mat (1).
• For a racing yacht where performance is paramount and budget allows, CFRP is the justified choice; GRP suits leisure boats where cost is more important than optimum weight (1).
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using wearable electronic textiles in professional sports clothing compared with conventional sportswear.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of advantages (real-time biometric monitoring — heart rate, motion, temperature; personalised training data; no need to wear separate devices; potential injury prevention) and disadvantages (durability under washing and stretching, higher cost, data privacy concerns, battery life, laundry and care complications). Judgement about the balance of benefits and barriers for professional versus consumer use.
Secure: Two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with some technical context (e.g. conductive yarns, encapsulation, washing limitations); conclusion present.
Developing: Points mostly listed; limited development; one side stronger.
Emerging: Simple advantages and disadvantages with minimal explanation; no judgement.
[8 marks — levels-based]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the role of the reinforcement in a composite material?
options: To bind the components together and distribute loads
To provide high strength and stiffness to the composite
To protect the material from UV degradation
To allow the composite to be moulded into complex shapes

knowledge_checks.q: Which composite is used by Airbus in aircraft wing structures because of its high stiffness-to-weight ratio?
Geotextiles are permeable fabrics used in _____ engineering to separate, filter, reinforce or drain soil.
Micro-fibres have a very fine diameter that creates billions of tiny air pockets, making them effective at _____ management in sports clothing.
Match each composite or textile to its key application:
right: Boat hulls and car body panels
Laid in the ground to separate and drain soil in road construction

flashcard_questions.a: A material made from two or more components with different properties combined to give superior performance to either alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two components of CFRP?
flashcard_questions.a: Carbon fibre reinforcement and an epoxy resin matrix.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Airbus use CFRP in aircraft structures rather than steel?
flashcard_questions.a: CFRP has a higher strength-to-weight ratio — it is lighter for the same strength, reducing fuel consumption.

flashcard_questions.q: What property of Kevlar makes it suitable for body armour?
flashcard_questions.a: Very high toughness — it absorbs impact energy by deforming rather than shattering.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the reinforcement material in GRP?
Name one advantage GRP has over CFRP for boat hull manufacture.
flashcard_questions.a: GRP is cheaper and can be applied by hand lay-up without specialist autoclave curing equipment.

flashcard_questions.q: What are technical textiles designed for?
flashcard_questions.a: Performance and function rather than appearance or aesthetics.

flashcard_questions.q: What do geotextiles do when laid in the ground under a road?
flashcard_questions.a: They separate the sub-soil from the gravel base while allowing water to drain through.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do micro-fibre fabrics work well in sports clothing?
flashcard_questions.a: Their very fine diameter creates a dense structure that wicks moisture away from the skin effectively.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a breathable waterproof membrane (e.g. expanded PTFE) keep rain out while letting sweat escape?
flashcard_questions.a: Its pores are small enough to block liquid water droplets but large enough to let water vapour pass through.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one method of embedding electronics into a textile without making it rigid.
flashcard_questions.a: Weaving conductive metallic yarns into the fabric to create a flexible circuit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main challenge in making wearable electronics durable in clothing?
flashcard_questions.a: The electronics must survive washing, stretching and the mechanical stresses of repeated wear.

glossary_terms.definition: A material made from two or more constituent materials with different properties that, when combined, produce a material with superior properties to either component alone.
A synthetic para-aramid fibre with extremely high tensile strength and toughness, used in body armour, cut-resistant gloves and structural composites.
A composite material consisting of glass fibre reinforcement embedded in a polyester or epoxy resin matrix, commonly used for boat hulls, car body panels and storage tanks.
Textile materials manufactured primarily for their technical performance and functional properties rather than aesthetic qualities.
